Local Ballot Measures – Proposition A
A – Charter Changes Affecting Various City 
Departments and Commissions
Digest by the Ballot Simplification Council
The Way It Is Now: The Charter is the City’s constitution 
and establishes the organization, powers, and 
responsibilities for many City departments. The Charter 
and other voter-approved laws also create many City 
commissions and advisory bodies and describe their 
powers, duties, membership and removal rules, and 
reporting requirements.
Over time, some of these laws have become obsolete.
The Charter and most laws passed by the voters can only 
be changed with voter approval.
The Proposal: Proposition A would align the Charter with 
how some City departments currently operate, change 
some processes, and eliminate or reorganize certain 
commissions and advisory bodies. Proposition A would 
require the Board of Supervisors to amend voter-approved 
laws to enact some of these changes.
Proposition A would:
•	 change the language of the Charter to reflect how some 
City departments currently operate in order to clarify 
responsibilities and update rules, procedures, and 
reporting requirements.
•	 change some processes. For example: allowing legal 
settlements to be approved by resolution instead of by 
ordinance.
•	 require a task force to meet every ten years to 
recommend changes to commissions.
•	 eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and 
advisory bodies by, for example: eliminating some 
commissions and advisory bodies, combining and 
renaming some advisory bodies, and moving some 
commissions and advisory bodies from the Charter into 
the Municipal Code.
A “YES” Vote Means: If you vote “yes,” you want 
to amend the Charter to align it with how some City 
departments currently operate, change some processes, 
eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory 
bodies, and require the Board of Supervisors to amend 
voter-approved laws to enact some of these changes.
A “NO” Vote Means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to 
make these changes.
Controller’s Statement on “A”
City Controller Greg Wagner has issued the following 
statement on the fiscal impact of Proposition A:
Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by 
the voters, in my opinion, it would have a moderate impact 
on the cost of government, saving $365,000 to $450,000 
annually. Additional costs and savings are dependent on 
the decisions that the Mayor and Board of Supervisors 
make through the normal budget process.
The proposed Charter amendment (1) modifies boards, 
commissions, and advisory bodies; (2) changes 
departmental operations and reporting requirements; 
(3) changes how the Board of Supervisors must 
approve settlements or dismissals of legal proceedings 
recommended by the City Attorney; (4) removes 
provisions allowing disciplinary action against non-Police 
and Fire striking employees; and (5) makes other edits 
and changes to the Charter and past voter-approved 
ordinances. The Charter amendment may reduce required 
staff time to support boards, commissions, and advisory 
bodies—freeing staff to work on other government 
functions.
The proposed Charter amendment creates cost savings 
ranging from $365,000 to $450,000 annually by eliminating

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition A
MAYOR LURIE & SUPERMAJORITY OF SUPERVISORS 
SAY YES ON PROP A TO CLEAN UP OUR 
OUTDATED CHARTER.
About every 30 years, City Hall sets aside its differences 
to clean up old, broken, and conflicting parts of our city’s 
governing document called the city charter.
Department heads, commissions, and the public suggest 
changes through a transparent, months-long process. The 
mayor and a supermajority of the Board of Supervisors 
agreed on 110 small fixes that will help city government 
serve you better.
The fixes fall into four categories:
OUTDATED TECHNOLOGY
New technology can make old laws pointless. For 
example, the current system still requires the city to 
employ a bookbinder and to publish laws in daily print 
editions of the Chronicle that no longer exist.
WASTEFUL DUPLICATION
Sometimes two city departments are required to do the 
exact same job. For example, multiple departments being 
required to create the same report, forcing employees into 
busy work that wastes time and money.
ZOMBIE COMMISSIONS
Our bureaucracy has 60 advisory bodies and commissions 
that can’t be updated without a vote at the ballot. After 
decades the charter can end up with zombie commissions 
that serve no purpose. For example, the Sanitation and 
Streets Commission oversees a department that doesn’t 
exist, and the charter still references a Parking Authority 
that voters removed a decade ago.
CONFUSING OR BADLY WORDED LAWS
Lawmakers sometimes make typos and mistakes when 
writing legislation, leaving behind laws that are confusing 
or just don’t make sense. Prop A cleans up some of the 
worst examples.
VOTE YES ON PROP A THE CITYWIDE GOOD

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition A
The charter should be improved, but not at the expense 
of transparency, and checks on government power. There 
are grievous mistakes in Prop A that threaten participatory 
democracy by removing commissions put in place 
by voters.
Take independent oversight for November 2018 
Proposition C. The measure allows the Board of 
Supervisors to remove independent oversight with a 
majority vote. Prop C, “Our City, Our Home”, is a deeply 
vetted people’s initiative placed on the ballot by Coalition 
on Homelessness alongside over 700 housed/unhoused 
volunteers and supported by 215,491 voters. It is a tax 
on mega corporations to fund homeless solutions. Due 
to careful planning by the oversight body, the fund has 
housed over 8,400 people, including 2,800 children, 
thousands prevented from becoming homeless, and 
receiving behavioral health treatment services.
Rising rents up and down the west coast have skyrocketed 
homelessness. Unlike west coast cities without a local 
revenue measure, SF has seen a steady decline in street 
homelessness. Portland saw an enourmous 67% increase 
and San Diego a 26% increase in 2024. SF was poised 
to see exploding homelessness due to the pandemic, but 
planning by the oversight body staved that off.
While Prop C has been wildly successful, progress is 
at risk. Rising rents create a dire need for using funds 
to permanently solve and prevent homelessness. The 
oversight body is charged with digging into data and 
centering unhoused people’s needs including hidden 
needs of homeless children. Each year they struggle 
against Mayoral Administrations who favor ruling by sound 
bites, and shiny failed quick fixes over data driven proven 
solutions.
Prop A attempts to silence the voices of homeless people 
and their allies that challenge power, and this particular 
body was targeted only because of its effectiveness 
in doing so.
No on A.
Coalition on Homelessness
Prop A is a good government housekeeping measure 
that cleans up and modernizes San Francisco’s 
lengthy, outdated charter to serve you better.
Currently five separate, overlapping commissions oversee 
homeless services in San Francisco. None of them are 
removed by Prop A.
But right now, even small administrative updates to some 
of these commissions — like adjusting how often they 
meet, or the qualifications of their members — have to go 
before voters as a ballot measure.
Making such routine updates should not be delayed 
through an entire election cycle or require hundreds 
of thousands of dollars in campaign costs. Prop A lets 
the Board handle those small fixes through ordinary 
legislation instead.
Requiring a citywide election to fix a typo or fix outdated 
language isn’t democracy, it just makes City Hall less 
accountable for delivering results for voters.
Join us as we make San Francisco’s charter serve 
you better!
VOTE YES ON PROP A — THE GOOD GOVERNMENT 
CONSENSUS MEASURE
Board of Supervisors President Rafael Mandelman

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition B
Digest by the Ballot Simplification Council
The Way It Is Now: A municipal finance corporation 
(MFC) is a government-owned non-profit corporation that 
makes loans but does not take deposits. A public bank is a 
government-owned non-profit corporation that both makes 
loans and takes deposits.
There is no local law authorizing the City to create a 
municipal finance corporation or a public bank.
The Proposal: Proposition B would amend the City 
Charter to authorize the City to establish a municipal 
finance corporation if the City has sufficient funding and 
resources. After three years of operation, the municipal 
finance corporation may become a public bank.
The MFC would make loans but would not take deposits. 
If the MFC becomes a public bank, the public bank would 
make loans and also take deposits.
The MFC and public bank would provide services 
to support:
•	 affordable housing development,
•	 affordable homeownership,
•	 small business development,
•	 environmental sustainability, and
•	 environmental justice.
These services would be available to individual City 
residents and to projects and businesses located 
in the City.
Under Proposition B, the MFC and public bank would 
each be governed by a board of directors. Each board 
would be appointed and overseen by its own oversight 
commission. The members of each oversight commission 
would be appointed by the Board of Supervisors, Mayor, 
Treasurer-Tax Collector, Controller, and City Attorney.
A “YES” Vote Means: If you vote “yes,” you want 
to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance 
corporation and a public bank.
A “NO” Vote Means: If you vote “no,” you do not want 
to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance 
corporation and a public bank.
Controller’s Statement on “B”
City Controller Greg Wagner has issued the following 
statement on the fiscal impact of Proposition B:
Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved 
by the voters, in my opinion, it would not directly impact 
the cost of government as the Charter amendment 
does not require the City to create a Municipal Finance 
Corporation (MFC) that could transition into a Public Bank. 
However, if the City moves forward with establishing a 
MFC and subsequently a Public Bank, as authorized by 
the proposed Charter amendment, the costs would be 
significant, ranging from approximately $310 million to 
$460 million over an eight-year period, according to 2023 
Reinvestment Working Group (RWG) estimates, which 
could be significantly higher or lower depending on interest 
rates and changing economic conditions.
The proposed Charter amendment sets up the governance 
framework for a new MFC and Public Bank. If the Charter 
amendment is approved, and the Treasurer-Tax Collector 
determines that adequate funding exists, the MFC and an 
MFC Oversight Commission may be established. In the 
Shall the City amend the Charter to authorize the City to establish a municipal 
finance corporation and a public bank?
This measure requires 50%+1 affirmative votes to pass.

event the MFC becomes financially sustainable, which is 
not guaranteed, the MFC may request state and federal

The funding required to set up an MFC could cost 
approximately $4 million annually for approximately one 
year or longer, depending on when the MFC is set up, 
excluding capitalization costs. These costs include the 
cost to hire staff, staff salaries, legal services, supporting

administrative operations.
In 2022, the County Local Area Formation Commission 
convened the RWG to develop a business and governance 
plan to establish a non-depository lending corporation. 
According to a 2023 report of the RWG, costs to capitalize 
and fund the MFC could cost approximately $26 million in 
the first year and increase to $30 million annually by the 
third year for a total of $90 million for the first three years 
of the MFC. The RWG explored a variety of capitalization 
and funding levels including cumulative totals of $45 million 
to $242 million over the first three years. Capitalization 
and funding costs could be financed by City grants and 
forgivable loans which are unlikely to be repaid. The 
capitalization and funding costs are choices dependent on 
future decisions by the MFC Board of Directors and future 
policy and budget decisions by the Mayor and the Board 
of Supervisors. The costs associated with establishing an 
MFC may be significantly higher or lower than the 2023 
RWG estimates.
In the event the MFC becomes financially sustainable and 
receives regulatory approval to operate as a depository 
bank, it may become a Public Bank. The cost to operate 
a Public Bank would be approximately $80 million in year 
4, decreasing to approximately $30 to $40 million annually 
for a total of approximately $220 million over years four 
through eight. These costs include capital funds and 
operating costs, including staff salaries, office leases, 
technology, and administrative costs. The Public Bank 
may use its income to fund its operating costs if available, 
requiring less funding appropriated by the City.
Finally, the MFC and Public Bank would require an MFC 
Oversight Commission or Bank Oversight Commission 
which could cost between $550,000 to $600,000 annually 
for staff salaries, commissioner stipends, and operating 
costs. There is a high degree of uncertainty in the cost 
to government of establishing an MFC or Public Bank. 
There may be significant unforeseen costs to the City in 
the event the Public Bank is not financially sustainable. 
The proposed Charter amendment gives a high degree 
of independence to the Oversight Commissions and the 
Board of Directors, such that the City would have limited 
control over the MFC’s or Public Bank’s financial outcomes 
and decisions on how funds would be used.
Note that the proposed amendment would change the 
duties of the Controller’s Office, which has prepared this 
statement.

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition B
Prop B will ensure that a San Francisco Public Bank 
is fiscally responsible, independent from political 
influence, and serves San Francisco’s priorities.
A Public Bank puts the people of San Francisco over 
private profits to finance the things we need. The 
shareholders would be the people of San Francisco, so 
we benefit not only from our bank’s profits but also the 
San Francisco projects it supports.
Prop B is a crucial step in creating a Public Bank. A Public 
Bank will provide affordable loans for:
•	 Affordable housing development,
•	 Affordable homeownership,
•	 Small business development,
•	 Environmental sustainability, and
•	 Environmental justice.
Prop B ensures that the Public Bank will be run by 
banking professionals, not politicians, and creates a 
public oversight body, so every San Franciscan has the 
opportunity to monitor and provide input. A public bank 
is about making sure San Franciscans’ money benefits 
San Franciscans.
Passing Prop B now allows us to take advantage of the 
time-limited state law that enables local cities to create 
public banks. A public bank creates a powerful new tool to 
address some of our city’s most urgent priorities. Public 
banking is a proven development model. Globally 25% 
of banking assets are held in public banks, and Germany 
holds 40% of its banking assets in public banks.
Prop B establishes the purpose and structure of a public 
bank. Prop B is not a tax, and will not raise taxes for 
San Franciscans.
The San Francisco Foundation

Proposition B asks San Francisco voters to create a

proven demand, and at a time when the City already faces 
massive budget shortfalls.

financial risks using public resources. The City’s own

dollars would be needed to capitalize such an institution. 
Proposition B provides none of that capital. It simply builds 
the structure and leaves taxpayers holding the bag later.

small businesses through existing programs, nonprofit 
lenders, and credit unions. Creating a new City-controlled 
bank adds bureaucracy, political risk, and potential 
conflicts of interest without solving the underlying problems 
of high costs and slow permitting.

experiment. Vote No on Proposition B.

San Francisco Public Bank, which could help fund 
housing, green energy, and small businesses, and sets 
rules to prevent the bank or its funds from being misused.
As the opponents point out, Prop B is NOT a tax and will 
not raise taxes on residents or businesses.

instability and risky lending, but that is untrue. Instead, it 
would be the most regulated bank in America, subject to all 
typical banking regulations of private banks, in addition to

and credit union ecosystem, making the most efficient use 
of taxpayer money.

energy, and supporting our small businesses.

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition C
Digest by the Ballot Simplification Council
The Way It Is Now: The City has a Housing Trust Fund 
(HTF) to support the creation or preservation of affordable 
housing and affordable home ownership. Every year, 
the City provides funding to the HTF, and the annual 
contribution is adjusted up or down based on changes in 
the City’s unrestricted General Fund revenue. Last year, 
the City contributed $50.8 million to the HTF.
The City may use HTF funds for:
•	 building, purchasing, and improving affordable housing;
•	 downpayment assistance loans for households earning 
up to 120% of Area Median Income (AMI) and for 
emergency first responders;
•	 assistance to households earning up to 120% of AMI to 
improve their housing and avoid housing loss;
•	 grant programs for specific types of neighborhood 
improvements; and
•	 administrative costs.
The Housing Trust Fund that supports these programs is 
set to expire in 2043.
The Proposal: Proposition C would change how the City’s 
annual contributions to the Housing Trust Fund (HTF) are 
set, increase funding and expand programs for affordable 
housing, and extend the Fund’s expiration date.
•	 Starting in 2028, the City’s annual contribution would 
grow based on the greater of either:
•	 any increases in local property tax revenue, or
•	 the percentage increase in the unrestricted General 
Fund from the prior year.
The City would increase its contributions to the HTF until 
the annual contribution meets or exceeds $125 million. 
After that, annual increases are capped at 3% based on 
increases in the General Fund.
The City could pause contributions when a projected 
City deficit exceeds $250 million. This threshold 
would be adjusted each year based on changes in the 
General Fund.
The City could also reduce contributions by up to 
10% during years when the City may use its Rainy 
Day Reserve.
•	 Expand affordable housing programs by:
•	 increasing funding to create and preserve more 
affordable housing;
•	 raising the household income limit for downpayment 
assistance loans from 120% to 200% of AMI, and 
allow the Board of Supervisors to change that limit by 
ordinance;
•	 replacing the grant program for specific types of 
neighborhood improvements by authorized spending 
on affordable housing-related infrastructure such as 
sidewalks, streets, and utilities;
•	 extending the Fund’s expiration date from 
2043 to 2058.
A “YES” Vote Means: If you vote “yes,” you want to 
amend the Charter to change how the City’s annual 
contributions to the Housing Trust Fund are set, increase 
funding and expand programs for affordable housing, and 
extend the Fund to 2058.
A “NO” Vote Means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to 
make these changes.
Shall the City amend the Charter to change how the City’s annual 
contributions to the Housing Trust Fund are set, increase funding and 
expand programs for affordable housing, and extend the Fund to 2058?
This measure requires 50%+1 affirmative votes to pass.
C – Contributions to the Housing Trust Fund

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition C
Controller’s Statement on “C”
City Controller Greg Wagner has issued the following 
statement on the fiscal impact of Proposition C:
Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by 
the voters, in my opinion, it would have a significant impact 
on the cost of government of approximately $6 million 
in additional General Fund costs starting in Fiscal Year 
2028-29, growing over time to approximately $60 million 
annually by Fiscal Year 2034-35.
The proposed Charter amendment is projected to increase 
the existing Housing Trust Fund (Fund) General Fund 
spending mandate for affordable housing and extends the 
mandate by an additional fifteen years from 2043 to 2058. 
A General Fund spending mandate is a voter-adopted 
spending requirement that directs the government to 
appropriate funding for specific purposes in future years 
without identifying a new funding source. For context, 
voter-adopted spending requirements currently total 
approximately $2 billion, or 30%, of the approximately 
$7 billion General Fund sources. Extending the life of 
the Housing Trust Fund and increasing contributions as 
projected would reallocate funds that would otherwise be 
available in the General Fund.
The proposed Charter amendment modifies the required 
funding formula to accelerate the growth of the Fund 
until the annual contribution reaches $125 million, likely 
in Fiscal Year (FY) 2034-2035, at which point the growth 
of the fund could slow. For context, in FY2024-25, 
approximately $50 million was appropriated to the Fund. 
As compared to projected Fund contributions under 
current law, the proposed Charter amendment is projected 
to increase contributions to the fund by approximately $6 
million in FY2028-29 and $13 million in FY2029-30. In 
subsequent years, the General Fund cost of the proposal 
is projected to grow by an additional $9 million annually, 
reaching approximately $60 million in additional growth 
by FY2034-35, resulting in a total expected contribution 
of $125 million in FY2034-35. Without the Charter 
amendment, the required funding formula is projected 
to be approximately $65 million in FY2034-35. The 
additional $60 million under the proposed modified funding 
formula represents the additional money the City would 
be required to appropriate into the Fund in FY2034-35 
and subsequent years. The projected costs above do 
not assume temporary freezes or reductions in the City’s 
annual contribution to the Fund.
The proposed Charter amendment allows the Mayor or the 
Board of Supervisors to introduce ordinances during the 
annual budget process to temporarily freeze or reduce the 
City’s annual contributions. If the City projects a budget 
deficit exceeding $250 million, the annual contribution to 
the Fund may be temporarily frozen at the then-current 
amount. If the City is authorized to withdraw funds from 
the City Rainy Day Reserve, the annual contribution to the 
Fund may be temporarily reduced by up to 10%.
The fund may be used to (1) create, acquire, or rehabilitate 
affordable rental and ownership housing, (2) provide 
down payment loans and housing stabilization for 
qualified households meeting required income levels, 
and (3) fund housing-related infrastructure, including 
streetscape improvements. The Charter amendment 
removes obsolete language regarding (1) past allocations 
to the Fund, (2) eliminating the Fund before 2013, (3) how 
the Controller’s Office may determine General Fund 
Discretionary Revenue, and (4) discretion to reduce Fund 
contributions based on debt service for SB 2113 Affordable 
Housing Bonds. Additionally, the proposed Charter 
amendment eliminates the Complete Neighborhoods 
Infrastructure Grant Program, which has not been funded 
since FY2019-20.
This proposed amendment is not in compliance with 
a non-binding, voter-adopted City policy regarding 
voter-adopted spending requirements. The policy 
seeks to limit General Fund spending mandates which 
reduce General Fund dollars that could otherwise be 
allocated by the Mayor and the Board of Supervisors in 
the annual budget process. For context, voter-adopted 
spending requirements currently total approximately 
$2 billion, or 30%, of the approximately $7 billion General 
Fund sources.
Note that the proposed amendment would change the 
duties of the Controller’s Office, which has prepared this 
statement.
How “C” Got on the Ballot
On July 14, 2026, the Board of Supervisors voted 11 to 0 
to place Proposition C on the ballot. The Supervisors voted 
as follows:
Yes: Chan, Chen, Dorsey, Fielder, Mahmood, Mandelman, 
Melgar, Sauter, Sherrill, Walton, Wong.
No: None.

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition C
San Francisco’s housing crisis is simple: rents and 
home prices have climbed faster than paychecks, and 
teachers, nurses, and multigenerational families are 
being priced out of the neighborhoods they grew up in or 
serve. Proposition C won’t solve that alone, but it renews 
San Francisco’s most significant source of funding for 
affordable housing.
For over a decade, the Housing Trust Fund has been 
San Francisco’s foundation for building affordable housing, 
helping first-time buyers purchase a home, keeping first 
responders in the city they serve, and giving seniors a way 
to stay in their communities.
Prop C renews the Housing Trust Fund through 2058 and 
increases its annual funding to $125 million. Every year we 
wait, the fund stays capped while rents keep climbing.
Prop C does not raise anyone’s taxes. It reallocates money 
the City already collects, and it is fiscally responsible by 
design. Funding only grows when the City’s own property 
tax or general fund revenue grows. The City can pause or 
reduce contributions during a real budget deficit. This is a 
careful, sustainable plan, not a blank check.
That is why Prop C is a true consensus measure. It 
was placed on the ballot unanimously by the Board 
of Supervisors and supported by labor and housing 
advocates across the city.
Prop C will build and rehabilitate affordable housing, 
fund down payment assistance for teachers and first 
responders, provide rent assistance to prevent seniors 
from being displaced, convert vacant lots into real housing, 
and fund needed infrastructure.
Every dollar is legally dedicated to affordable housing and

It Couldn’t Do the Job It Had. Now It Wants a 
Bigger One.
San Francisco’s Housing Trust Fund was established in 
2012 to help working families afford housing. It has failed. 
Local reporting calls the fund “a letdown” and “an existing 
program that has yielded little.” Since the fund’s creation, 
the cost to build a single affordable unit in San Francisco 
has roughly doubled, running close to $1 million per 
unit today.
Instead of a fix, this measure doubles the fund’s size, locks 
it in for 30 more years, and stretches it thinner:
–	 Raises the homebuyer income cap from 120% to 200% 
of “median income” — up to $402,000 for a family of 
four, in a city where the real median household income 
is $141,000.
–	 Let’s the Board of Supervisors raise that cap again 
anytime, with no vote required.
–	 Opens the fund to new uses like city-owned “social 
housing” and co-ops, all competing for the same dollars.
–	 Swaps a specific, accountable neighborhood fund for a 
vague, open-ended one.
Nothing in the measure requires a single additional 
unit to get built. There’s no unit target. No benchmark. 
Meanwhile, San Francisco remains tens of thousands of 
units short of its own housing goals.
A program that already failed at one job doesn’t get fixed 
by giving it five new jobs and more money. Fix what’s 
broken first.
Vote No on C.
The San Francisco Republican Party
Proposition C renews and expands a program 
San Francisco voters already created: the Housing Trust 
Fund, dedicated to building affordable homes, helping 
teachers and first responders become homeowners, and 
keeping seniors from losing their housing.
It includes real fiscal guardrails. The City can freeze 
contributions during a genuine budget deficit and reduce 
them by up to 10 percent in years when it draws on the 
Rainy Day Reserve.
Funding only grows when the City’s own property tax or 
general fund revenue grow. This is not a blank check. It is 
a formula built for both growth and restraint. Every dollar 
is legally restricted to affordable housing, homeownership 
assistance, and rent relief.

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition D
YES
NO
Digest by the Ballot Simplification Council
The Way It Is Now: The San Francisco Board of 
Supervisors (Board) has 11 members. A measure can be 
either an ordinance to change the law or a declaration of 
policy. Under the City Charter, measures can be placed on 
the ballot in several ways, including:
•	 By a majority vote of the Board;
•	 By four or more Board members without a Board vote;
•	 By the Mayor without a Board vote; or
•	 By a signature initiative (petition) signed by at least 2% 
of the registered voters in San Francisco, currently about 
10,600 signatures.
Currently San Francisco has over 530,000 registered 
voters.
Signature initiatives usually appear on the ballot at the 
next regularly scheduled election.
Signature initiatives may call for an earlier “special” 
election on an ordinance if the petition is signed by at least 
10% of the votes cast for all candidates for Mayor in the 
last election. Currently, this is about 39,000 signatures.
Once a signature initiative is submitted to the Department 
of Elections, it cannot be withdrawn.
The Proposal: Proposition D would amend the Charter 
to increase the requirements to put measures on the 
ballot by:
•	 Increasing the number of signatures required to place a 
signature initiative on the ballot from 2% to 8% (currently 
from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures) of the 
registered voters in San Francisco.
•	 Increasing the number of signatures required to call 
a special election on an ordinance from 10% of the 
votes cast for Mayor in the last election to 10% of the 
registered voters in San Francisco. Currently, this is 
about 53,100 signatures.
Proposition D would allow signature initiatives to be 
withdrawn up to 102 days before the election.
Proposition D would also change the requirements to put 
measures on the ballot by:
•	 Removing the ability of four or more Board members to 
place a measure on the ballot without a Board vote;
•	 Removing the ability of the Mayor to independently place 
a measure on the ballot;
The Board could still place measures on the ballot by a 
majority vote.
A “YES” Vote Means: If you vote “yes,” you want to 
increase the requirements for signature initiatives from 2% 
to 8% of registered voters (currently from about 10,600 
to about 42,500 signatures), increase the requirements 
for special elections, allow signature initiatives to be 
withdrawn, and remove the ability of a minority of Board 
members or the Mayor to place measures on the ballot.
A “NO” Vote Means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to 
make these changes.
Shall the City amend the Charter to increase the requirements for signature 
initiatives from 2% to 8% of registered voters in San Francisco (currently 
from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures), increase the requirements for 
calling special elections, allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn before 
an election, and remove the ability of a minority of Board of Supervisors 
members or the Mayor to place measures on the ballot?
This measure requires 50%+1 affirmative votes to pass.

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition D
Controller's Statement on “D”
City Controller Greg Wagner has issued the following 
statement on the fiscal impact of Proposition D:
Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by 
the voters, in my opinion, it would have a minimal impact 
on the cost of government.
The proposed Charter amendment would (1) require the 
approval of a majority of the Board of Supervisors to place 
an ordinance on the ballot, (2) eliminate the Mayor’s ability 
to directly place an ordinance on the ballot, (3) increase 
the voter signature threshold for initiatives from 2% to 8% 
(currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures) 
of the registered voters in San Francisco, (4) allow 
proponents to withdraw a measure after it qualifies for the 
ballot, and (5) raise the threshold for special elections from 
10% of the votes for mayor in the last general municipal 
election to 10% of registered voters.
The proposed amendment is likely to reduce costs at 
levels that cannot be determined at this time. Since the 
proposed Charter amendment raises the voter signature 
threshold, fewer initiatives may qualify for the ballot which 
may reduce the volume of printed pages included in the 
voter information pamphlet (VIP). On average, each page 
in the VIP costs $11,400 to prepare, print, and distribute to 
all registered voters. The proposed increase in the voter 
signature threshold may also reduce the number of special 
elections called which would result in cost savings for the 
Department of Elections. The estimated minimum cost for 
a citywide special election is $5 million with a one-card 
ballot and less than 50-page VIP.
The proposed Charter amendment may impact the 
Department of Elections’ workload. It may result in a 
reduction in ballot ordinances which would reduce the 
associated workload for the Department of Elections—
freeing staff to work on other government functions. 
Conversely, the Department of Elections may see an 
increase in workload to validate more voter signatures for 
a measure to qualify for the ballot and to remove qualified 
measures at the proponents’ request.
How “D” Got on the Ballot
On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified 
that the initiative petition calling for Proposition D to be 
placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid 
signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot.
53,076 signatures were required to place an initiative 
Charter Amendment on the ballot. This number is equal to 
10% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent 
to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of 
the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative 
petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline 
showed that the total number of valid signatures was 
greater than the number required.

Paid Arguments in Favor
Fewer Measures. Better Decisions. 
San Francisco voters face some of the longest, most 
complicated ballots in California — 15 local measures in 
November 2024 alone, compared to 3 in Oakland and 1 
in San José. Since 1996, San Franciscans have voted 
on 418 local measures, nearly half placed on the ballot 
without the ordinary legislative process of public hearings 
and Board approval.
This reform comes straight from SPUR’s Charter for 
Change (2026), building on recommendations SPUR 
first raised in Designed to Serve (2024) and on SPUR’s 
long history of advocating for smarter, more deliberate 
lawmaking in San Francisco, including its sponsorship of 
2007’s ballot-sunshine reforms.
The measure ends the practice of the Mayor or just 
four Supervisors placing measures directly on the ballot 
without majority Board support — a power no other 
major California city grants. It raises the citizen signature 
threshold from 2% to 8% of registered voters, still lower 
than Oakland, San Diego, Sacramento, and most 
California cities. And it lets initiative sponsors withdraw 
measures before an election, opening the door to 
negotiated solutions instead of costly campaigns.
Complex policy deserves public hearings and negotiation, 
not an up-or-down vote squeezed between a dozen other 
measures. This measure lets City Hall do its job, reserving 
the ballot for issues that truly need a public vote.
Vote YES.
Sean Elsbernd
President/CEO SPUR (www.spur.org)

GOOD GOVERNANCE LEADERS AGREE PROP D WILL 
IMPROVE VOTER TRUST.
A healthy democracy depends on a ballot voters can trust 
— one with proposals made with real community support, 
not political maneuvering. San Francisco’s current system 
falls far short. It requires 80% fewer signatures than the 
state standard, meaning a small minority of politicians and 
private interests can flood the ballot with contradictory 
measures designed to confuse voters and settle political 
scores. We’ve seen how this plays out: instead of building 
coalitions and answering hard questions publicly, insiders 
can target a handful of supervisors to get a measure on 
the ballot.
Prop D protects the ballot from manipulation. It requires 
a majority of the Board of Supervisors or signatures 
from 8% of voters — much closer to the state’s 10% 
standard — and removes the mayor’s power to unilaterally 
place measures on the ballot, which no other California 
cities had to start with. It also lets proponents withdraw 
measures, allowing space to reach agreements or correct 
for flaws or unintended consequences instead of leaving 
voters to clean up the mess.
This is a structural fix for a structural problem: a process 
that currently rewards insider access instead of genuine 
coalition-building and public vetting. Good government and 
a functioning democracy means a ballot voters can trust. 
Prop D gets us there.

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition E
Digest by the Ballot Simplification Council
The Way It Is Now: The City Administrator’s Office is 
responsible for most of the City’s purchasing. However, 
authority for the City’s purchasing and technology is 
shared among the City Administrator’s Office, the Board of 
Supervisors, the Mayor, and some City departments.
•	 Rules Regulating Purchasing: The Board of Supervisors 
(Board) may adopt ordinances that set the rules 
about how the City selects contractors and enters into 
contracts for goods, services, construction, and grants 
(referred to below as Purchasing).
•	 Board Approval of Various Agreements: With some 
exceptions, the City’s Charter requires the Board 
to approve:
•	 Contracts and leases that bring in $1,000,000 or more 
in revenue to the City, and
•	 Contracts that cost the City $10,000,000 or more.
The Board must also approve certain amendments to 
these agreements.
•	 City Administrator’s Term: The Mayor appoints the 
City Administrator to a five-year term, subject to 
Board approval.
•	 City Administrator’s Authority: The City Administrator 
sets Purchasing rules and processes governing goods 
and services except for some goods and services of 
the Municipal Transportation Agency, Public Utilities 
Commission, Port Commission, and some arts 
departments. The City Administrator also oversees 
technology policies and manages disposal of City 
personal property for most departments.
The Proposal: Proposition E would:
•	 Rules Regulating Purchasing: Give the City 
Administrator exclusive authority to propose ordinances 
that change how the City selects contractors and enters 
into contracts for goods, services, construction, and 
grants (Purchasing). The Board and Mayor may not 
amend the ordinances, but they can:
•	 Approve or reject the ordinances within 60 days, or
•	 If no action is taken within 60 days, the ordinances 
would be approved.
Proposition E does not change the current Board 
authority for Purchasing ordinances that mainly address 
wages, workplace health and safety, utilization of local 
business, or labor agreements.
•	 Board Approval of Various Agreements: Increase the 
dollar amount requiring Board approval to:
•	 Contracts and leases that bring in $4,500,000 or more 
in revenue to the City,
•	 Contracts that cost the City $25,000,000 or more.
Starting in 2032, the City’s Controller would adjust these 
dollar amounts every five years for inflation.
Proposition E would require Board approval for major 
amendments to these agreements.
•	 City Administrator’s Term: Increase the City 
Administrator’s term from five to ten years.
•	 City Administrator’s Authority: The City Administrator 
would set Purchasing rules and processes for all 
goods, services, construction, and grants that all City 
departments must follow, except as limited by other 
laws. Most departments would now be subject to the 
Shall the City amend the Charter to give the City Administrator more authority 
by centralizing the City’s purchasing rules and processes, changing how the 
City approves purchasing rules, changing when contracts and leases require 
Board of Supervisors approval, and extending the City Administrator’s term?
This measure requires 50%+1 affirmative votes to pass.
E – City Administrator’s Authority and Changes 
to City Contracting

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition E
City Administrator’s authority regarding technology

A “YES” Vote Means: If you vote “yes,” you want to give 
the City Administrator more authority by centralizing the 
City’s Purchasing rules and processes, changing how the 
City approves Purchasing rules, changing when contracts 
and leases require Board approval, and extending the City 
Administrator’s term.
A “NO” Vote Means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to

Controller’s Statement on “E”
City Controller Greg Wagner has issued the following 
statement on the fiscal impact of Proposition E:
Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by 
the voters, in my opinion, it would have a minimal impact 
on the cost of government, although at a level that cannot 
be determined at this time.
The proposed Charter amendment would (1) give the 
City Administrator the exclusive authority to introduce 
ordinances that govern City contracting, with some 
exceptions; (2) grant the City Administrator the authority 
to set Citywide rules for contracting; (3) provide the City 
Administrator the authority to establish policies, standards, 
and practices for technology uses across departments; 
(4) extend the City Administrator’s term from five to ten 
years; (5) increase the Board of Supervisors’ approval 
threshold from $1 million to $4.5 million for revenue 
generating contracts and real property lease agreements; 
and (6) increase in the Board of Supervisors’ approval 
threshold from $10 million to $25 million for expenditure 
contracts.
The proposed Charter amendment gives the City 
Administrator greater authority to set contract standards, 
by introducing ordinances or adopting rules, regulations or 
policies, which may allow for greater efficiencies in citywide 
contracting. The proposed amendment establishes a more 
unified City procurement approach, which may result 
in reduced costs for the purchase of goods or services 
and staff time savings in the long run. The amendment 
may result in changed staffing but does not specify 
organizational or staffing changes within the City.
The proposed Charter amendment also increases 
the Board of Supervisors’ contract approval monetary 
thresholds. These changes may reduce the amount of time 
the Board of Supervisors spend reviewing contracts and 
the time department staff spend preparing for the Board of 
Supervisors’ review, freeing the Board of Supervisors, their 
staff, and department staff to work on other government 
functions, although at a level that cannot be determined at 
this time.
How “E” Got on the Ballot
On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified 
that the initiative petition calling for Proposition E to be 
placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid 
signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot.
53,076 signatures were required to place an initiative 
Charter Amendment on the ballot. This number is equal to 
10% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent 
to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of 
the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative 
petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline 
showed that the total number of valid signatures was 
greater than the number required.

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition E
Over decades, San Francisco’s governing system - or city 
charter - has increasingly grown to reward city insiders. 
Mayor Lurie is leading a citywide coalition to make the 
system more accountable to everyday San Franciscans.
Clean Up City Hall is a package of Props A, D, E and F to 
improve neighborhood services, speed up permitting and 
reduce wasteful spending so we can invest in our great city.
PROP E SLASHES WASTE IN CITY CONTRACTING.
It can cost more than $25,000 to run a single contracting 
process. Basic purchases take years to deliver. Costs 
balloon out of control. That’s because every year 
San Francisco hands out more than $5 billion in contracts 
with no limited oversight or accountability. The system 
creates waste at every level and is easily exploited.
STOPS CORRUPT DEALMAKING. Investigators have 
caught six department heads running contracting schemes 
in the last five years. Multiple department heads have gone 
to prison. E empowers a professional City Administrator to 
set transparent standards so contracts are awarded based 
on who is best for the job, not who is best connected.
MORE ACCOUNTABILITY FOR BETTER RESULTS. 
“San Francisco pays thousands of businesses and 
nonprofits but doesn’t have a contracting system built for 
results. E ensures public dollars are invested in better and 
faster city services instead of lost to waste and delay.” - Ben 
Rosenfield, former San Francisco Controller
STRONGER CHECKS AND BALANCES. The mayor or 
a board majority can reject proposed contracting changes 
within 60 days, ensuring accountability runs through the 
entire system.
San Francisco works best when we work in coalitions 
together. Please join the citywide coalition to make the 
system accountable to all!

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition E
The current Board of Supervisors refuses to enact Mayor 
Daniel Lurie’s core priorities—to cut the deficit, trim 
bureaucracy, centralize contracting and hold department 
heads accountable. However Lurie, instead of challenging 
head-on the far-left socialists and obstructionist ideologues 
of his own party to get pragmatist Supervisors elected, 
treats the system of checks and balances itself as the 
enemy. He raised millions for paid signature gatherers to 
rewrite the City Charter and concentrate power in his hands.
This is the authoritarian temptation. Fearing radicals 
inside their own coalition, leaders turn against institutional 
constraints that limit their personal power. SPUR stated the 
impulse with chilling clarity: a mayor should “resolve issues 
through leadership rather than at the ballot”—translation: by 
mayoral decree. Democratic procedure just gets in the way.
That same impulse drives presidents who prefer executive 
orders to the harder work of defeating “in name only” 
members of their own party who block their agenda.
One measure expands City Administrator authority, raising 
the dollar threshold for Supervisor approval of major 
contracts. Another revives deputy mayors—a patronage 
system exposed by Quentin Kopp and abolished by voters 
in 1991—while amplifying the mayor’s power to hire, 
fire and reorganize. The third quadruples the signature 
requirement for citizen initiatives, after Lurie himself 
used the low bar he now seeks to close, locking the door 
behind him.
Most of what Lurie claims these changes would deliver 
could be achieved through legislation and regular order if 
he led his own party toward fiscal discipline, drove the most 
ideological members off the Board and fought the increasing 
far-left extremism infecting Democrat leadership. Instead, 
he flirts with the same breed of authoritarianism.
Don’t be a piker.
Vote No on D, E, and F.
Larry S. Marso, Esq.
PROP E IS IS ABOUT ENDING WASTE AND 
CORRUPTION IN CITY CONTRACTING
Under our current system, San Francisco became an 
international punch line when it was announced that 
one public toilet in Noe Valley would cost $1.7 million 
dollars to build.
Under our current system, multiple city employees, 
including 6 department heads, were investigated for running 
contracting schemes that landed some of them in prison.
Under our current system, it costs more than $25,000 to run 
a single contracting process, and simple purchases drag on 
for years.
But the city continues to hand out $6 billion in contracts a 
year without the oversight and accountability that common 
sense demands.
How the city buys staplers, builds public restrooms, or 
purchases software can’t be a political football.
Prop E empowers a professional City Administrator to set 
clear, transparent rules for who gets city contracts. It’s a 
necessary step to end waste, fraud, and ballooning costs 
that frankly should have been done decades ago.
City Hall insiders want to keep our current system because 
it works for them. But San Francisco voters have made it 
clear that it’s time for a change.
Join us in bringing sanity back to purchasing and 
contracting.
Mayor Daniel Lurie

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition E – Paid Arguments
Paid Arguments in Favor
Cut the Red Tape. Deliver Services Faster.
San Francisco spends more than $5 billion a year on 
contracts — for everything from homeless services 
to street repairs — under purchasing rules scattered 
across more than 100 sections of city code, requiring 
8.5 months to 1.5 years to complete a single contract. 
Small businesses and nonprofits, especially minority- and 
women-owned firms, are hit hardest.
This measure implements the recommendations of 
SPUR’s 2025 Purchasing Power report and 2026 Charter 
for Change — research built on SPUR’s century-long 
commitment to making San Francisco government work 
efficiently for the people it serves.
The measure puts one official, the City Administrator, in 
charge of proposing purchasing rule changes, subject to 
Board rejection within 60 days. It brings departments like 
the PUC and SFMTA under consistent citywide purchasing 
oversight. And it updates Board-approval contract 
thresholds, unchanged since 1996, to reflect nearly three 
decades of inflation.
Existing protections for minority- and women-owned 
business participation and labor standards on city 
contracts are untouched, as is the Board’s budget authority 
over the City Administrator’s office and the Mayor’s ability 
to remove the City Administrator.
The result: faster contracting, lower administrative costs, 
and a system that’s finally navigable for the nonprofits and 
small businesses serving San Francisco’s most vulnerable 
residents.
Vote YES.
Sean Elsbernd
President/CEO SPUR (www.spur.org)

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition F
Digest by the Ballot Simplification Council
The Way It Is Now: The Mayor is the chief executive 
officer of the City. The Mayor directly supervises nearly 
50 City departments, which are established by Charter 
or ordinance. Most City departments are established 
by Charter.
•	 Transfer of Functions: The Mayor can transfer 
responsibilities between departments established 
by ordinance, as long as the Board of Supervisors 
(Board) does not object. The Mayor cannot transfer 
responsibilities for departments established by 
the Charter.
•	 Deputy Mayors: The Mayor cannot hire deputy 
mayors to supervise most departments established by 
the Charter.
•	 Department Heads: In most cases, the Mayor 
must select a department head from candidates 
recommended by the board or commission that 
oversees that department. Usually, the board or 
commission can fire the department head, but the 
Mayor cannot.
•	 Commissioners: In addition to the Mayor, the Board 
and other officials appoint members to City boards and 
commissions. Appointed members can usually only be 
suspended or removed if the member engaged in official 
misconduct or committed certain felonies.
The Proposal: Proposition F would amend the Charter to 
allow the Mayor to do the following:
•	 Transfer of Functions: Transfer responsibilities between 
most departments or combine departments under a 
single department head, regardless of whether the 
Department was established by ordinance or Charter 
and as long as the Board does not object. The Mayor 
cannot eliminate any responsibilities established by 
Charter. The Mayor could also assign the oversight of 
these transferred responsibilities to that department’s 
commission. The Mayor cannot transfer responsibilities 
of these departments:
•	 City Administrator, Controller, Board of Appeals, 
Port, Airport, Asian Art Museum, Fine Arts Museums, 
San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency, 
Public Utilities Commission, Civil Service Commission, 
Department of Human Resources, Retirement Board, 
Health Service System, Department of Elections, 
Ethics Commission, or departments headed by other 
elected officials. 
The responsibilities of the Department of Police 
Accountability cannot be transferred to the Police 
Department, and the responsibilities of the Sheriff’s 
Inspector General cannot be transferred to the Sheriff.
•	 Deputy Mayors: Hire deputy mayors to supervise most 
departments established by the Charter.
•	 Department Heads: Hire some and fire most department 
heads without board or commission involvement. The 
Mayor cannot hire or fire certain department heads 
that are exempt (see List of Exemptions in Words You 
Need To Know).
•	 Commissioners: In addition to the Mayor, the Board 
and other officials who appoint board and commission 
members could remove them at any time without cause. 
This does not apply to the Board of Appeals, Civil 
Service Commission, or Ethics Commission. The Mayor 
cannot eliminate any board or commission established 
by the Charter.
Shall the City amend the Charter to expand the Mayor’s authority to transfer 
responsibilities between departments, hire deputy mayors, and hire some 
and fire most department heads; and to allow City officials to remove 
members of boards and commissions without cause?
This measure requires 50%+1 affirmative votes to pass.

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition F
A “YES” Vote Means: If you vote “yes,” you want to 
expand the Mayor’s authority to transfer responsibilities, 
hire deputy mayors, hire some and fire most department 
heads, and allow City officials to remove members of 
boards or commissions without cause.
A “NO” Vote Means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to 
make these changes.
Controller’s Statement on “F”
City Controller Greg Wagner has issued the following 
statement on the fiscal impact of Proposition F:
Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by 
the voters, in my opinion, it would have a minimal impact 
on the cost of government, although at a level that cannot 
be determined at this time.
The proposed Charter amendment would (1) expand the 
Mayor’s authority to hire and remove most departments 
heads; (2) allow most commissioners to be removed at will 
by their appointing authority; (3) authorize the Mayor to 
reorganize departments and adjust reporting relationships 
within the executive branch, subject to potential rejection 
by the Board of Supervisors; and (4) allow the use of 
deputy mayors. 
The proposed Charter amendment authorizes the Mayor 
to utilize deputy mayors. The average annual cost for 
a deputy mayor would be approximately $250,000. 
The proposed Charter amendment allows the Mayor 
to restructure departments and reorient reporting 
relationships within the executive branch. The potential 
costs or savings incurred for such changes cannot 
be determined without knowing which departments 
would be involved and how the departments would be 
restructured. For example, in Fiscal Year 2022-23 when 
the Department of Sanitation and Streets merged into 
the Department of Public Works, the Controller’s Office 
estimated cost savings of $3.5 million in the first year 
and $2.5 million in the second year of the merger. Cost 
savings came from removing duplicative administrative 
and information technology staff, departmental leadership, 
and one-time and ongoing costs, such as equipment and 
professional services.
How “F” Got on the Ballot
On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified 
that the initiative petition calling for Proposition F to be 
placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid 
signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot.
53,076 signatures were required to place an initiative 
Charter Amendment on the ballot. This number is equal to 
10% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent 
to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of 
the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative 
petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline 
showed that the total number of valid signatures was 
greater than the number required.

Over decades, San Francisco’s governing system - or city 
charter - has increasingly grown to reward city insiders. Mayor 
Lurie is leading a citywide coalition to make the system more 
accountable to everyday San Franciscans.
Clean Up City Hall is a package of Props A, D, E and F to 
improve neighborhood services, speed up permitting and 
reduce wasteful spending so we can invest in our great city.
PROP F TACKLES CITY HALL CORRUPTION.
The current system allows departments to operate as 
independent fiefdoms instead of coordinated parts of 
government. It protects the insiders instead of holding them 
accountable. Six department heads have been indicted or 
investigated for corruption in the last decade. The mayor can 
only hire and remove a handful of department heads when 
self-dealing is exposed or they fail to do their job.
CLEAR LINES OF ACCOUNTABILITY. Allowing the mayor to 
hire and remove most of their department heads will ensure 
city officials are accountable to the public.
BETTER ORGANIZED DEPARTMENTS FOR BETTER 
RESULTS. Better organized and more accountable 
departments will deliver faster permits, cleaner streets and 
projects done on time and on budget.
EXPOSES SELF-DEALING. “Departments that act as their 
own kingdoms are where corruption can grow. F makes it 
clear that every department head is ultimately accountable 
to the people of San Francisco” - Louise Renne, former 
San Francisco City Attorney & CA Deputy Attorney General

of Supervisors will still have oversight over city departments 
and a majority of the Board can reject any changes the 
mayor makes. Watchdog commissions like Ethics and police 
oversight remain fully independent.
San Francisco works best when we work in coalitions 
together. Please join the citywide coalition to make the system 
accountable to all!

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition F – Paid Arguments
Paid Arguments in Favor
Clear Accountability for City Government
San Francisco’s Mayor is the city’s chief executive 
but today directly appoints and removes only 6% of 
department heads. Responsibility is scattered across 
dozens of commissions and overlapping approval 
processes, making it nearly impossible for voters 
to know who is accountable when city government 
succeeds or fails.
This measure is drawn directly from SPUR’s 2026 Charter 
for Change report and its 2024 Designed to Serve 
research — the product of SPUR’s decades of nonpartisan 
work studying how San Francisco’s city government 
actually functions, and how it can work better.
The measure gives the Mayor authority to appoint and 
remove most department heads, while preserving Board 
approval for the Controller, City Administrator, and Human 
Resources Director. It allows the Mayor to organize their 
office effectively, including using deputy mayors — a basic 
tool most big‑city mayors already have. And it lets the 
Mayor propose reorganizing departments, subject to Board 
rejection within 60 days, so the government can adapt 
without a citywide election every time.
Critically, independent oversight is protected: the Ethics 
Commission, Elections Commission, Controller, City 
Administrator, Board of Appeals, Civil Service Commission, 
and elected officials like the City Attorney and District 
Attorney are all exempted.
When authority and accountability are aligned, voters can 
judge elected officials’ performance at the ballot box. This 
measure ends the finger‑pointing.
Vote YES.
Sean Elsbernd
President/CEO SPUR (www.spur.org)

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition G
Digest by the Ballot Simplification Council
The Way It Is Now: Sunset Dunes Park is an open 
recreational space that replaced the Great Highway 
between Lincoln Way and Sloat Boulevard (Upper Great 
Highway) and is closed to private vehicles at all times.
Sunset Dunes Park (former Upper Great Highway) 
is open to emergency vehicles, official government 
vehicles, intra-park transit shuttle buses, and similar 
authorized vehicles.
The Proposal: Proposition G would close Sunset 
Dunes Park from Monday at 4:00 a.m. through Friday at 
6:00 p.m., unless a holiday falls on a weekday, in order to 
reopen the roadway known as the Upper Great Highway to 
private vehicles during that time.
The Upper Great Highway will remain open to emergency 
vehicles, official government vehicles, intra-park transit 
shuttle buses, and similar authorized vehicles.
Proposition G would require the City to obtain all 
necessary approvals, including any permits required by the 
California Coastal Act or from other government agencies, 
to reopen the roadway known as the Upper Great Highway 
to private vehicles.
A “YES” Vote Means: If you vote “yes,” you want to close 
Sunset Dunes Park from Monday at 4:00 a.m. through 
Friday at 6:00 p.m., unless a holiday falls on a weekday, 
in order to reopen the roadway known as the Upper Great 
Highway to private vehicles during that time.
A “NO” Vote Means: If you vote “no,” you do not want the 
City to make these changes.
Controller’s Statement on “G”
Deputy City Controller ChiaYu Ma has issued the following 
statement on the fiscal impact of Proposition G:
Should the proposed Ordinance be approved by the voters 
and the roadway is open to private vehicles, in my opinion, 
it would significantly increase the cost of government by 
approximately $9.8 million in one-time capital costs and 
by approximately $500,000 to $1.9 million annually. The 
cost of the proposed Ordinance, should it be approved 
Shall the City close Sunset Dunes Park from Monday at 4:00 a.m. through 
Friday at 6:00 p.m., unless a holiday falls on a weekday, in order to reopen 
the roadway known as the Upper Great Highway to private vehicles during 
that time?
This measure requires 50%+1 affirmative votes to pass.
G – Allowing Private Vehicles on the Upper Great 
Highway in Sunset Dunes Park

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition G
by the voters, is dependent on decisions that the Mayor 
and Board of Supervisors make through the budget 
process and operational decisions made by departments, 
as an ordinance cannot bind future Mayors and Boards 
of Supervisors to provide funding for this or any 
other purpose.
The proposed initiative ordinance would amend the Park 
Code to restrict private vehicles on the Upper Great 
Highway between Lincoln Way and Sloat Boulevard 
from Friday at 6:00 PM until Monday at 4:00 AM and 
on holidays.
Depending on future operational decisions made by 
City departments, the proposed Ordinance could result 
in annual cost increases ranging from $500,000 to 
$1.9 million. This includes traffic signal maintenance 
costs, annualized roadway maintenance and replacement 
costs, and an additional cost for sand removal and dune 
reshaping. The sand removal and dune reshaping would 
cost approximately $100,000 and $1.5 million more each 
year, which represents an increase over current levels of 
service. Sand removal costs are highly dependent on the 
defined level of service, weather conditions and funding 
availability, which results in a wide range of potential costs. 
For context, sand removal and dune reshaping for Sunset 
Dunes Park was approximately $290,000 in FY 2024-2025 
and $330,000 in FY 2025-2026. In prior years when 
the roadway was open to vehicles on weekdays, actual 
expenditures for sand removal and dune reshaping was 
approximately $860,000 in FY 2022-2023 and $420,000 
in FY 2023-2024. The proposed Ordinance would also 
result in decreased staffing needs and maintenance of 
Sunset Dunes Park as a park during weekdays, reducing 
costs and freeing staff to work on other functions. For 
context, staffing at Sunset Dunes Park costs approximately 
$300,000 annually for 1.5 full-time-equivalent positions.
Additionally, the proposed Ordinance would likely result in 
increased, one-time capital project costs of approximately 
$9.8 million. This would include approximately 
$750,000 to remove existing park elements and restore 
roadway segments, $8.8 million in new traffic signals 
at 8 intersections, and $200,000 for temporary and 
permanent restriping and signage. A full signal upgrade 
would be necessary approximately every 30 years. 
Installation of signals at the intersection of the Upper 
Great Highway and Sloat Boulevard would result in 
changes to the Ocean Beach Climate Change Adaptation 
Project, which could result in additional project costs for 
redesigning elements of the planned plaza.
Finally, the proposed Ordinance would require a coastal 
development permit. Applying for the coastal development 
permit may prompt additional requirements, including 
studies or permit conditions, that may increase the cost of 
government, although at a level that cannot be determined 
at this time.
How “G” Got on the Ballot
On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified 
that the initiative petition calling for Proposition G to be 
placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid 
signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot.
10,615 signatures were required to place an initiative 
ordinance on the ballot. This number is equal to 2% of the 
registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate 
Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures 
submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior 
to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that 
the total number of valid signatures was greater than the 
number required.

neighborhood campaign.

and holidays.

off-road amenities, every day of the week.

for our communities.

stake, we have a duty to respond.

Paid Arguments in Favor
Is it fair for people from one neighborhood to deprive 
another neighborhood of a key artery? To close a major 
roadway against the wishes of the great majority of its 
residents? A roadway used by school buses, Paratransit,

to everyone — not just bicyclists, skateboarders, and 
health-conscious people.

no diversity of use; no equity for local residents; and no 
inclusion of the disabled, who best enjoy the scenic view 
as passengers.
Currently, it’s only accessible to a limited segment of the 
population. For everyone else: KEEP OUT.
It discriminates against the frail and physically disabled; 
against locals who can no longer easily cross the 
City N—S. Most of all, it discriminates against every 
San Francisco resident who might enjoy a scenic 
drive along the Pacific Ocean, on their own or with 
out-of-town visitors.
The opponents of Proposition G want the Great Highway 
all to themselves. Yet it remains woefully underused Mon—
Fri; and is practically devoid of people on rainy days.
Proposition G doesn’t eliminate Sunset Dunes Park. It 
merely seeks full utilization (multi-use, Mon—Fri) of a key 
thoroughfare lying atop the Westside Transport sewage 
aqueduct (which must be maintained regardless).
When Prop K was introduced, it was framed as “Park = 
Good”, voters not fully aware of the high cost in lost use for 
locals and visitors alike. 
Proposition G aims to remedy this imbalance by 
restoring the optimal use of the Great Highway for the 
common good.
J. Gregson

Supervisor Alan Wong: Prop G Makes Transit More 
Efficient 
Closing the Great Highway did not make traffic 
disappear. It simply pushed traffic onto other streets, 
including residential streets never designed to carry the 
same volume of vehicles.
For Westside residents, these consequences affect 
everyday life. Trips that once moved efficiently along 
the Great Highway are now diverted through slower 
neighborhood streets with more stops, intersections, and 
turns. Residents spend more time getting to work, taking 
their children to school, reaching medical appointments, 
and traveling across the Westside.
Slower, less direct routes have environmental 
consequences. Vehicles travel farther and spend more 
time stopping, idling, and accelerating. That means 
additional vehicle miles traveled and emissions in 
residential neighborhoods. Closing the Great Highway did 
not eliminate these trips; it made them slower, less direct, 
and more disruptive.
Recreation and transportation already existed side by 
side along our coast. Ocean Beach and the recreational 
trail provided substantial opportunities for walking, biking, 
and enjoying the coast. San Francisco also has an 
extensive network of parks and open spaces. Permanently 
removing a useful transportation corridor comes with a 
real tradeoff when recreational opportunities already exist 
alongside it.
The previous compromise offered a practical balance: 
weekday vehicle access while maintaining recreational use 
at other times. And it worked.
Good transportation policy should improve the 
network as a whole, not simply relocate congestion. 
Returning to a practical compromise would restore an 
important transportation connection, reduce unnecessary 
traffic on residential streets, shorten trips, and better 
balance mobility, recreation, and quality of life for Westside 
residents.
Prop G makes our transportation system more 
efficient.
Vote Yes on Prop G
Supervisor Alan Wong

Vote Yes on G: The Numbers Tell a Different Story
We’ve been told that allowing weekday vehicle access on 
the Great Highway will lead to higher sand removal costs. 
But Public Works’ own records tell a different story.
Records obtained through a Sunshine request show 
that from 2011 through 2025, sand removal expenses 
between Lincoln Way and Sloat Boulevard were less than 
$400,000 per year.
Now, with the Great Highway closed to vehicles 
24/7, costs are going up, not down. In just the first 
six months of 2026, sand removal cost $281,785. If 
that pace continues, 2026 will exceed $500,000, the 
most expensive year for sand removal, without cars 
on the road.
Since the 24/7 closure, the frequency of sand removal 
has doubled, from twice monthly to weekly. It is more 
labor‑intensive, requiring hand‑shoveling around structures 
to move sand where heavy equipment can reach it.
And sand removal isn’t the only expense. The 24/7 closure 
has changed how people access the dunes. Without traffic 
and pedestrian signals directing people to designated 
crossings, increased foot traffic over fragile dunes 
damages native plants, worsens erosion, and increases 
the need for costly dune reshaping.
Protecting our natural beach environment protects 
taxpayers too. When dunes are protected from

Paid Arguments Against
An Expensive Step Backward for San Francisco’s Coast
Voters already settled this. In November 2024, 55% 
of San Francisco approved Proposition K, permanently 
protecting Sunset Dunes park as open space and 
closing the former Upper Great Highway to cars. This 
measure would undo that decision and bring an end to a 
beloved park.
San Francisco didn’t stumble into this park by accident. 
In 2012, SPUR published the Ocean Beach Master Plan, 
the first comprehensive vision for removing cars from this 
stretch of coastline and restoring it for people and coastal 
resilience. For more than a decade, SPUR has led the 
public process — with the National Park Service, the 
SFPUC, and the State Coastal Conservancy — that made 
Sunset Dunes park possible.
It’s also a bad deal for taxpayers. This eroding roadway 
closed unpredictably up to 65 days a year before Prop K, 
costing hundreds of thousands of dollars annually. Bringing 
it back would add $500,000–$1,900,000 a year in ongoing 
maintenance costs, plus $9.8 million to rebuild the road, 
all for an unreliable road that dead-ends into permanent 
closure at Sloat Boulevard regardless.
This park has become one of San Francisco’s most-loved 
public spaces. Reversing course would eliminate 
multilingual, multigenerational programming and increase 
pollution runoff into a sensitive coastal ecosystem — 
solving nothing.
This issue has been exhausting for San Franciscans. 
Six years of debate, two citywide votes, two lawsuits, 
three appeals. Enough is enough — we are saying No 
to Proposition G, and no to wasteful ballot measures on 
issues we’ve already settled as a city.
Spending nearly $10 million to remove a playground, 
a skate park, and public art from public land is just 
irresponsible, especially when San Francisco is being 
forced to make budget cuts.
Vote No.
Sean Elsbernd
President/CEO SPUR (www.spur.org)

Local Ballot Measures – Proposition G – Paid Arguments
Here’s the traffic truth: since the park opened, traffic is 
not more dangerous than it was before, and we’re still 
getting everywhere we need to go.
•	 Major arteries continue to keep drivers moving. Data 
shows travel times on key routes like Sunset Blvd and 
19th Ave saw nearly no change after Sunset Dunes 
opened—varying by at most two minutes even at rush 
hour, with some trips actually faster. Traffic volumes on 
Sunset Blvd remained below pre-pandemic levels.[1]
•	 Travel times for commuters are as predicted before 
Prop K: An independent review commissioned by the 
San Francisco Chronicle found that the travel time 
for the most impacted trip was four minutes longer at 
weekday rush hour, with many trips unaffected.[2]
•	 Sunset streets remain safe and calm: A separate 
independent analysis found that “there’s no evidence 
of increased street mayhem around the closed Great 
Highway. In fact, it’s the opposite” and “injury collisions 
on D4 streets dropped below 2019 and 2024 levels.”[3]
Meanwhile, the Great Highway closed up to 65 days each 
year due to sand accumulation, and the southern end is 
closing permanently.
There is no traffic reason to close Sunset Dunes park. 
Don’t close a great park to rebuild an unreliable road.
[1]: “Outer Sunset Traffic Data Report”
[2]: SF Chronicle, “Has Great Highway Closure Made

Closure and Sunset District Traffic”

Digest by the Ballot Simplification Council
The Way It Is Now: The Municipal Railway (Muni) 
provides public transit in San Francisco, including bus, 
light rail, streetcar, and cable car. Muni provides over 
500,000 rides per weekday. Muni service is funded by 
transit fares and local, state and federal sources, but not 
through a parcel tax.
State law limits the total revenue, including tax revenue, 
that the City may spend each year. The voters may 
approve increases to this limit for up to four years.
Owners of rent-controlled residential property in the City 
are generally limited in what costs they can pass onto 
their tenants.
The Proposal: Starting July 1, 2027, and continuing 
until June 30, 2042, Proposition H would fund Muni 
service through a new annual parcel tax on real estate in 
San Francisco. The tax would be adjusted annually for 
inflation.
The proposed 2027 tax rates would be:
•	 Single-Family Residential Parcels:
•	 A base tax of $129.
•	 For buildings with more than 3,000 square feet of 
building area:
•	 $0.42 per square foot between 3,001 and 
5,000, and
•	 $1.99 per square foot over 5,000.
•	 Multifamily Residential Parcels:
•	 A base tax of $249.
•	 For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of 
building area:
•	 $0.195 per square foot over 5,000.
•	 This tax is capped at $50,000 per parcel.
•	 Non-Residential Parcels:
•	 A base tax of $799.
•	 For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of 
building area:
•	 $0.76 per square foot between 5,001 and 50,000,
•	 $0.84 per square foot between 50,001 and 
250,000, and
•	 $0.99 per square foot over 250,000.
•	 This tax is capped at $400,000 per parcel.
•	 Mixed-Use Parcels:
•	 A base tax of $799.
•	 For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of 
building area:
•	 A combination of the marginal rates for residential 
and non-residential parcels above.
•	 This tax is capped at $400,000 per parcel.
•	 Parcels with No Buildings:
•	 No base tax.
•	 $392 for land area over 2,000 square feet.
The tax would not apply to:
1.	Properties or portions of properties not required to pay 
standard property taxes; and
2.	Single Room Occupancy (SRO) units and their shared 
facilities such as kitchens or bathrooms.
Most homeowners aged 65 or older living in their primary 
home would get a discount or pay no tax.
Revenues from the tax would only be used for Muni 
service and administering the tax. In addition to the annual 
required audit by an independent auditor, an annual report 
and efficiency review would be required.
This measure would increase the City’s spending limit for 
four years.
Shall the City fund Muni service through a new annual parcel tax on real 
estate at rates ranging from $129 per parcel up to a maximum of $400,000 per 
parcel, depending on the type of property and its size and adjusted annually 
for inflation, for estimated revenue of $177 million a year for 15 years?
This measure requires 50%+1 affirmative votes to pass.
H – Parcel Tax to Fund Muni Operations

Owners could pass up to 50% of the tax onto tenants in 
rent-controlled units where the rent was set before June 1,

A “YES” Vote Means: If you vote “yes,” you want the City 
to fund Muni service through a new annual parcel tax on
